subject: RCOS Step 5 — the selection bus
task: Build the pluggable selection interface GPT's round-7 ruling names as Step 5: the immutable rcos-selection/1 protocol, candidate-set integrity, exactly one selector (explicit@1), the fresh scope=execute handoff for the winner, and provenance pinning — and stop there.

spec.file: workspace/default/partsnap-rcos/GPT-REPLY-7-20260917.md (outside this repo — the ruling is quoted verbatim below so this receipt stands alone)
spec.ruling_verbatim: Ruling: Step 5 is the selection bus, not the selection brain. Build the immutable protocol, candidate integrity, explicit selector, fresh execute-eligibility handoff, and stop there.
spec.invariant: Selection may choose only among capabilities already proven eligible to compete. Selection never grants execution authority.
spec.flow_verbatim: REGISTRY + EVAL STATE -> ELIGIBILITY(scope=compete) -> eligible candidate set -> SELECTOR -> selection decision -> ELIGIBILITY(scope=execute) <- fresh decision for winner -> INVOCATION KERNEL
spec.why_the_second_check_verbatim: That second eligibility check is important. A MAY_COMPETE decision must never authorize execution.
spec.three_locked_meanings_verbatim: selection says WHICH / eligibility says MAY / kernel says CAN EXECUTE SAFELY
spec.minimum_shape_verbatim: {schema, selection_id, selector:{id,version}, candidates:[{capability_id, capability_version, eligibility_decision_id, eligibility_sha256}], status, selected_capability_id, selector_input_sha256, integrity}
spec.core_is_stupid_on_purpose_verbatim: Core verification is deterministic and deliberately stupid. It does not judge whether the choice was smart. It does not judge whether the task semantically matched. It does not judge whether another candidate was better. It does not judge whether a rationale sounds convincing. Those are selector-quality questions for later evals.
spec.selector_input_is_opaque_verbatim: Selector-specific input stays opaque to core. Core must not define a universal vocabulary containing task_text, intent, similarity, domain, scores.
spec.no_reuse_semantics_verbatim: Selection is not reuse. Selection is not invocation. Selection is not success. Even: selected does not mean: invoked or: successfully reused. Leave the Step-1 invariant alone.
spec.direct_invocation_verbatim: Do not make selection mandatory for direct invocation.
spec.non_goals_verbatim: Do not build: LLM router / learned router / ranking / similarity / task interpretation / cost-aware selection / latency-aware selection / workflow planner / fallback selector / automatic retries / authority / truth envelope / dependency planning / PartSnap semantics
spec.must_fail_closed_verbatim: Also pin: explicit(nonexistent) / explicit(ineligible legacy cap) / tampered candidate eligibility / tampered selection / selection of candidate not in set / compete decision supplied directly to kernel. All must fail closed.
spec.dogfood_plan_verbatim: Under eval + scope=compete: reuse-ledger eligible / agents-md-compactor eligible. Create a candidate set containing both. Then: explicit(reuse-ledger) -> selected reuse-ledger. Request fresh: eligibility(reuse-ledger, scope=execute, eval context). Then execute it. Separately: explicit(agents-md-compactor) -> selected successfully -> executes successfully -> eval remains FIX. Again proving: ELIGIBLE != GOOD / SELECTED != GOOD / EXECUTED != GOOD. Quality remains exclusively the eval runner's concern.
spec.sequence_adjustment_verbatim: After this ships, I would not immediately build an intelligent selector. Step 6 should remain the truth/evidence envelope. The empty selector slot can stay empty. That is healthy.
spec.why_wait_verbatim: Once truth and later authority exist, an intelligent selector will receive a much better-defined world: eligible actions + grounded state + explicit objective — rather than raw prompts plus a giant capability registry.

verdict_basis: All 18 items of the round-7 ship bar PASS in a self-contained harness (evidence/2026-09-18-step5-selection/shipbar-verify.js, all_pass: true), re-run on the frozen tree after the last edit. The bus is measured end-to-end against the real registry with nothing stubbed: 22 capabilities -> 2 executable -> 2 may compete -> 2 on the ballot -> 2 explicitly selectable -> 2 execute-eligible at purpose eval -> 0 at purpose normal. Two live dogfood invocations came through a selection and received a fresh scope=execute decision before running; one of them completed and its own gates still say 'fix', which is the point — ELIGIBLE != GOOD, SELECTED != GOOD, EXECUTED != GOOD. Six refusal shapes fail closed, five of them as sealed status=blocked invocations and one (no decision at all) as a plain error. The registry and traces are byte-identical across the whole step and no reuse_count moved. Suite 87/87 across 11 files, Step 1-4's own 15-item verifier still 15/15.

ship_bar.item: Selection consumes only verified scope=compete eligible decisions.
ship_bar.evidence: The control ballot was built from two real scope=compete decisions and both pins were re-verified from disk. Five refusals, each with its verbatim basis: a scope=execute decision offered as a candidate ('has scope execute — a candidate must be a scope=compete decision, because competing is the only question selection is allowed to ask'); a compete decision that says no ('does not permit competition: not_executable'); a decision id naming no artifact ('no such eligibility decision artifact'); a string that is not a decision id; and a decision whose bytes were edited after it was written ('does not verify: decision integrity mismatch — the decision was edited after it was written; ineligible decision carries no reason'). Tampered bytes restored afterwards.

The decision-producing functions called by the selection module are an empty list — selection cannot ask the eligibility question because it is not given one to ask. The proof is behavioural: one decision was recorded as eligible, and the same capability asked afresh with a different caller context (purpose=normal) answers false with [candidate_not_allowed, provenance_asserted, no_ship_eval] — while the selection, which carries no context and no purpose, follows the recorded verdict and returns 'selected'. The opposite decision is refused as a candidate. What verification does read is the registry, to confirm the decision names a capability that exists at the recorded version: a reference check, never a verdict.

schema constant 'rcos-selection/1'. Five distinct edits each caught by the integrity hash — status_basis edited, status flipped, a candidate sha replaced, a whole candidate removed, the integrity value itself edited — all with the same first problem: 'selection integrity mismatch — the selection was edited after it was written'. Bytes restored after each edit and the artifact verifies again. Write-once enforced: a second create for the same id throws 'selection already exists — selections are write-once and never rewritten'.

ship_bar.item: The candidate set is exact and hash-pinned.
ship_bar.evidence: candidate_set_sha256 recomputed independently from the artifact matches the recorded value (081a790d8d7d0ab88cf40d2e33b6e1a206243f1849bbfc77b7e48763658df219). Exactness: candidates.length equals the number of decisions supplied, one entry per decision, in the order supplied. Adding a third candidate changes the hash. A duplicate capability in the set is refused: 'a candidate set is a set, and two pinned decisions for one capability is an ambiguity the protocol will not guess its way out of'. A swapped candidate sha is caught three ways (integrity mismatch, candidate_set_sha256 mismatch, and the per-candidate eligibility_sha256 mismatch against the decision artifact it names); a lied-about version is caught as 'decision names version 0.1.0, selection pins 9.9.9'.

ship_bar.item: Core validates membership, not semantic quality.
ship_bar.evidence: A deliberately bad selector was injected: one that ignores its input entirely and picks the last candidate with the basis 'I picked the last one. No reason.' — the core selected it and recorded the basis verbatim. Another stated a claim the core cannot check ('agents-md-compactor is clearly the best match for this task') and the artifact still verifies. The judgement vocabulary present in the shipped core is an empty list. What the core checked is that the named capability is one of the candidates — nothing else. What it did not check: whether the choice was smart, whether the task semantically matched, whether another candidate was better, whether the rationale is true.

Installed selectors: exactly ['explicit']. The shipped selector exposes id, version, validateInput, select. Naming a selector that does not exist is refused ('no selector X is installed — this build ships exactly one: explicit'), and naming a version that does not exist is refused too ('selector explicit is version 1, not 2'). The future selector names GPT listed are absent as code; only the word 'planner' appears, in prose, in a comment. The empty slots are named in prose and implemented nowhere — the healthy state the ruling asked for.

ship_bar.item: Selector implementations use a replaceable interface.
ship_bar.evidence: The core calls exactly: id, version, validateInput(input) -> string[], select({candidates, selector_input}) -> {status, selected_capability_id, reason}. A foreign selector (probe-abstain@3) was injected into the core without editing the core — 'core_edited_to_do_this: false' — and it appears in the artifact as {id: 'probe-abstain', version: '3'} with status 'abstained', and its own input rule was enforced by the selector itself, not the core: 'selector probe-abstain@3 rejected its input: probe-abstain needs {ok: true}'. The artifact verifies.

ship_bar.item: Selector-specific input is opaque to the core.
ship_bar.evidence: An exotic input object (nested arrays, a key with spaces, unicode, an arbitrary key named frobnicate) was stored verbatim and hash-pinned; input_sha256 recomputed from the input alone matches (90939fb49cb9c4f111357274c9db559d32ee46d1a6aa795708dbbd7bce3fd86f) and the artifact verifies. The universal vocabulary keys present in the core: an empty list. The only closed vocabulary in the build is explicit@1's own, and it enforces it itself: unknown key ('selector input.task_text: unknown field — explicit@1 accepts exactly one key, capability_id'), missing key, and wrong type all refused by the selector.

ship_bar.item: The five statuses are structurally distinct.
ship_bar.evidence: Canonical order: selected, abstained, ambiguous, no_candidates, failed. A selector may return only the first three. All five were produced: selected (basis 'requested agents-md-compactor is in the eligible candidate set'), abstained, ambiguous, no_candidates (basis 'the candidate set is empty — no scope=compete eligible decision was supplied, so no selector was convened'), and failed (basis 'selector p-throws@1 threw: kaboom'). Only 'selected' names a capability; the other four all carry null. A selector attempting to return a core-only status is refused, and a selector that throws is sealed as failed rather than crashing the core.

ship_bar.item: Selection does not grant execution permission.
ship_bar.evidence: Six refusal shapes measured, with the verbatim basis for each: a compete decision offered as the authorizing decision; a valid selection and no decision at all; a selection that chose a different capability; a selection that abstained; a selection id that names no artifact; a selection whose bytes were edited. The load-bearing discovery is the refusal SHAPE: when the kernel has a decision and/or a selection to reason about it SEALS the attempt as an invocation with status 'blocked' (ok: true, refusal text in status_basis) rather than returning an error — the audit trail shows what was tried. Only the missing-decision case is a plain error, because there is nothing to seal. The control with a real execute decision and the same selection completed. The three meanings, recorded: selection WHICH, eligibility MAY, kernel CAN EXECUTE SAFELY.

ship_bar.item: The winner receives a fresh scope=execute decision.
ship_bar.evidence: Two live dogfood invocations came through a selection and each carries an execute decision minted AFTER the selection, from a different decision family than the competing ones: inv_20260918T041803Z-2ca0d3 (reuse-ledger, selection sel_20260918T041756Z-75466d decided at 04:17:56.704Z, execute decision elig_20260918T041803Z-fb9c84 created at 04:18:03.786Z, fresh: true, status completed) and inv_20260918T043148Z-d5b980 (agents-md-compactor, selection sel_20260918T043119Z-cdd68f at 04:31:19.348Z, execute elig_20260918T043148Z-4741e6 at 04:31:48.784Z, fresh: true, status completed). Live asymmetry measured in the same instant: both capabilities are may_compete_at_purpose_eval true and may_execute_at_purpose_normal false, for the same three reasons — a MAY_COMPETE decision must never authorize execution, and here it demonstrably does not.

ship_bar.item: The kernel still requires execute eligibility.
ship_bar.evidence: An execute decision that says no (reasons: candidate_not_allowed, provenance_asserted, no_ship_eval) is sealed as blocked with the basis 'eligibility decision does not permit execution: ...; eligibility decision was made for purpose normal, which does not authorize a eval-mode invocation'. The same refusal shape holds for a compete decision offered to the kernel. The control — a real, eligible, purpose-matching execute decision — completes. Eligibility is therefore still load-bearing at the kernel boundary and selection did not become a substitute for it.

ship_bar.item: Optional selection provenance can be pinned into invocation artifacts.
ship_bar.evidence: inv_20260918T043148Z-d5b980 pins selection_id sel_20260918T043119Z-cdd68f, its sha256 (11f76976fb8aa48ee97fc3fd5d8d555f3adc8c94af1655702d9a5e1dc38b5ea5), and a block {selector, status, selected_capability_id, candidates, path}. Verification re-hashes 11 artifacts and passes. Editing the pinned selection breaks verification with two problems — 'selection changed since the invocation was written' and the selection's own integrity mismatch — and restoring the bytes verifies again. Selection problems therefore include per-candidate problems, which is why a probe home must carry the candidate decisions.

ship_bar.item: Direct 'rcos run <id>' does not require artificial selection.
ship_bar.evidence: A direct invocation ran with selection_id null and selection_block null and completed; the direct CLI run exited 0 and printed no selection line. Selection is provenance a caller may attach, never a step a caller must perform.

ship_bar.item: Selection does not change reuse_count or traces.
ship_bar.evidence: The trace-and-reuse identifiers present in the selection module: an empty list. What the selection module does write is exactly one file: selections/<selection_id>/selection.json, written once and never rewritten. Across the harness, which convened the selector live three times (one selected reuse-ledger, one abstained, one no_candidates): registry sha identical before and after (2bd52677...), traces sha identical (6f0a97d1...), trace lines 98 before and 98 after, reuse_counts_moved: []. Selection is not reuse: selected is not invoked, and invoked is not successfully reused. The traces file has moved since the step-5 start (96 lines then, 98 now) but not inside this harness and not by this step's commit — see item 18.

ship_bar.item: No semantic routing, ranking, model, or planner exists.
ship_bar.evidence: A 24-word vocabulary was searched over the selection module's code and the CLI's select surface, with comments stripped first so prose cannot mask or fake a hit: similarity, cosine, embedding, tfidf, keyword, rank, score, heuristic, predict, learn, weight, llm, openai, anthropic, gpt, prompt, planner, intent, task_text, semantic, route, router, classify, nearest. Hits in the selection code: none. Hits in the CLI select surface: none. How a choice is actually made: explicit@1 compares one string the caller supplied against the candidate capability ids — there is no other way for a capability to be chosen in this build. Deferred and absent: LLM router, learned router, ranking, similarity, task interpretation, cost-aware selection, latency-aware selection, workflow planner, fallback selector, automatic retries.

ship_bar.item: Existing Step 1-4 invariants and tests remain green.
ship_bar.evidence: Suite exit 0, 87 tests, 87 pass, 0 fail, 0 skipped, across 11 test files (the counters as printed: 'tests 87' / 'pass 87' / 'fail 0' / 'skipped 0'). Step 4's own 15-item verifier was re-run from a temp-dir copy so its evidence of record (sha 84037b4a6c604bb44ea11f70b4b41e238ba7dcd103544c4be37229e3c59ab2f8) was never overwritten: all_pass true, 15 items, and every item verdict unchanged from the recorded ones. The rerun home was removed afterwards.

ship_bar.item: The registry remains unchanged unless a separately justified migration requires otherwise.
ship_bar.evidence: The registry and the traces are byte-identical before and after this harness (2bd52677... and 6f0a97d1...), nothing under registry/ or traces/ is left uncommitted, and this step's own commit 6c34ee2 touched neither file — its paths are README.md, bin/rcos, lib/invocation.js, lib/selection.js, tests/selection.test.js. The step-start values this is measured against are re-derived from that same commit rather than remembered, and the harness's own copies of them are asserted to agree with git. The registry does differ from the value at the step-4 commit (0379300d...) and from the value at this step's start, and the divergence is attributed rather than dropped: every commit in the window that touched registry/ or traces/ is a study-loop commit (9410e0e 2026-09-18, dc07607 2026-09-18, b969ee6 2026-09-18, 60f564e 2026-09-17), machine-written on the loop's own schedule. Read that way, "the registry remains unchanged" is a claim about this step, and it holds at both levels: the step's commit touches neither data file, and the harness moves neither byte.

statuses.why_structurally_distinct: the statuses are not labels on one shape — they are five different answers to five different questions. no_candidates is 'there was nothing to choose from' (the core never convened a selector). failed is 'a selector existed and broke'. ambiguous is 'a selector existed and could not choose'. abstained is 'a selector chose not to choose'. Only selected answers 'which one', and only that answer can be carried forward.

refusal_shapes.the_rule: When the kernel has a decision and/or a selection to reason about, it seals the attempt as an invocation with status 'blocked' — ok: true, with the refusal text in manifest.status_basis — so the audit trail records what was tried, not merely that it failed. A missing eligibility decision is the one plain error (ok: false), because there is nothing to seal.
refusal_shapes.why_this_matters: a refusal that returns nothing leaves no evidence a refusal happened. Sealing turns 'someone tried to run X without authority' into an artifact you can find later.

must_fail_closed.spec_verbatim: explicit(nonexistent) / explicit(ineligible legacy cap) / tampered candidate eligibility / tampered selection / selection of candidate not in set / compete decision supplied directly to kernel
must_fail_closed.explicit_nonexistent: abstained, basis: requested '<id>' is not in the eligible candidate set [agents-md-compactor, reuse-ledger]. (Not 'failed': naming a capability the caller believes in but that is not on the ballot is a refusal to choose, and the ballot is the whole world a selector is allowed to know.)
must_fail_closed.explicit_ineligible_legacy_cap: offering a real capability that is not eligible to compete — 20 of the registry's 22 capabilities were offered to explicit@1 by name in the sweep, and all 20 abstained. A compete decision that says no cannot even enter the ballot: 'does not permit competition: not_executable'.
must_fail_closed.tampered_candidate_eligibility: caught: 'candidate eligibility decision ... does not verify: decision integrity mismatch — the decision was edited after it was written; ineligible decision carries no reason'. Selection verification additionally re-derives candidate_set_sha256 and re-hashes each pinned decision.
must_fail_closed.tampered_selection: caught by the artifact's own integrity hash, by the kernel's selection_sha256 comparison against the manifest ('selection changed since the invocation was written'), and by selection-verify.
must_fail_closed.selection_of_candidate_not_in_set: refused by the core: a selector that names a capability outside the candidate set does not get its answer recorded as selected — the core checks membership and the choice is refused. (Membership is the ONLY thing the core judges.)
must_fail_closed.compete_decision_supplied_directly_to_ke: blocked, basis: 'eligibility decision was asked at scope compete — only a scope=execute decision authorizes execution, and a scope=compete decision means "may stand for election", not "may run"'.

dogfood_runs.result: ELIGIBLE != GOOD, SELECTED != GOOD, EXECUTED != GOOD. A capability can win an election, be freshly authorized, run to completion — and still be judged a FIX by the only thing allowed to judge quality. The bus moved the work; the eval judged it. That separation is the deliverable.

Nothing is mutated: no registry byte, no trace line, no reuse_count. A selection that was later re-run or re-thought is a new artifact with a new id; none is ever rewritten.

verification_harness.note: shipbar-verify.js is the gate. It is self-contained, it seeds every probe from the real home with cpSync, it sabotages only temp directories, and it re-runs Step 4's verifier from a copy so Step 4's evidence of record is never overwritten.
verification_harness.was: no selection bus existed: there was no artifact type, no candidate set, no selector interface, and the kernel took an eligibility decision only
verification_harness.now: 18/18 PASS, all_pass: true, on the frozen tree
verification_harness.why_not_just_accept_it: five of the eighteen items are negative claims (no recomputation, no authority, no reuse movement, no semantic routing, no registry movement). A negative claim that is only asserted is a check that cannot fail. Each is therefore measured against a control that would move if the claim were false: the same capability asked twice with different contexts, a registry and trace hash taken before and after the whole harness, a 24-word vocabulary scan run over comment-stripped source, and this step's own commit read path by path. "Unchanged registry" is deliberately read as "unchanged by this step" and not "equal to the step-start sha": an autonomous study loop commits machine-written registry and trace updates on its own schedule, so a frozen-equality gate would fail for a reason that is not evidence about the selection bus, and bumping the constant until it passed would be worse. What is gated is what this step owns — the harness window is byte-identical for both files, nothing under them is uncommitted, and commit 6c34ee2 touches neither — and what is not gated is still recorded: every window commit that did move the data is listed by sha, date and subject.
